guide.title: Hypertensive Emergencies
guide.lead: A high number alone isn't an emergency; damage to an organ is. Find the organ that's suffering and treat that. Don't chase the BP down in the field. Pregnancy, the aorta and the brain are the three you can't miss.

sections.title: Urgency or emergency?
sections.question: Systolic above 180 and/or diastolic above 120 mmHg. Any acute organ damage?
items: Brain: severe headache, confusion, seizures, stroke signs, vision loss
Aorta: tearing pain to the back
Pregnancy, or up to 6 weeks after delivery
sections.no: Urgency: calm, recheck, transport for review. No field BP lowering.
sections.yes: Emergency: treat the damaged organ, emergency transport to the right centre.

sections.title: Treat the organ, not the number
rows: Left lateral, dim lights, seizure precautions; magnesium (ALS)

groups.title: Aortic dissection
items: Sudden tearing pain to the back
Arm BP difference above 20 mmHg or a pulse deficit

groups.title: Preeclampsia
items: BP 140/90 or more after 20 weeks; severe 160/110 or more
Headache, visual spots, right upper abdominal pain, edema

groups.title: Cushing's triad
items: High BP with widening pulse pressure
Raised intracranial pressure: don't lower BP

quiz.q: What separates a hypertensive emergency from an urgency?
Ripping chest pain to the back; BP 186/94 right arm and 142/78 left. Diagnosis and destination?
options: Aortic dissection: emergency transport to a centre with cardiothoracic surgery
quiz.explanation: An arm difference above 20 mmHg is a red flag.

options: Raised intracranial pressure with risk of herniation
quiz.explanation: The high BP is protecting brain perfusion.

options: Systolic above 180 and/or diastolic above 120 mmHg

quiz.q: Should EMS lower a high BP in the field?
options: No: treat the organ problem and transport
quiz.explanation: Fast drops can cause stroke and organ ischemia.

quiz.q: Preeclampsia is new BP of 140/90 or more after:
Best position for a woman with preeclampsia in late pregnancy?
quiz.explanation: Takes the uterus off the vena cava.

quiz.q: Can preeclampsia appear after the baby is born?
options: Yes, up to 6 weeks after delivery
quiz.explanation: Ask about recent delivery in any woman with headache and high BP.

quiz.q: Which drug should you withhold when aortic dissection is suspected?
quiz.explanation: It can worsen bleeding if the aorta is torn.

flashcards.question: Hypertensive urgency vs emergency
flashcards.answer: Both: systolic above 180 and/or diastolic above 120 mmHg. Emergency has acute organ damage (brain, heart, aorta, kidneys, eyes, pregnancy).

flashcards.question: Signs of organ damage
flashcards.answer: Brain: severe headache, confusion, seizures, vision loss, stroke signs. Heart: chest pain, pulmonary edema. Aorta: tearing pain to the back.

flashcards.question: Common trigger for a hypertensive crisis
flashcards.answer: Stopping medicines: rebound after clonidine or beta-blockers.

flashcards.question: Lower BP in the field?
flashcards.answer: No. Treat the organ problem and transport; fast drops cut perfusion.

flashcards.question: Cushing's triad
flashcards.answer: High BP (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia, irregular breathing = raised intracranial pressure. Don't lower the BP.

flashcards.question: Aortic dissection: key features
flashcards.answer: Sudden tearing pain to the back, arm BP difference above 20 mmHg, pulse deficit, history of hypertension.

flashcards.question: EMS care in hypertensive emergency
flashcards.answer: Position of comfort, oxygen if hypoxic, treat the organ problem (aspirin for ACS, CPAP for edema), calm, transport to the right centre.

flashcards.question: Preeclampsia and eclampsia
flashcards.answer: New BP 140/90 or more after 20 weeks (severe 160/110 or more) with organ signs; up to 6 weeks after delivery. Eclampsia = seizures.

critical.scenario: A 55-year-old stopped his BP medicines 3 weeks ago. "Worst headache" for 2 hours, confused and not tracking your finger. BP 224/128. No chest pain or weakness.
critical.question: Urgency or emergency, and what do you do?

options.t: Emergency (brain involvement): supportive care, emergency transport, no field BP lowering
Urgency: no chest pain, so routine transport
options.f: Confusion and vision problems are organ damage.

options.t: Lower his BP quickly with whatever is available
Give his old medicines and leave him at home

critical.explanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy: the hospital lowers BP slowly with IV drugs and close monitoring.
critical.kpi: Differentiates hypertensive emergency from urgency and identifies CNS end-organ damage

critical.scenario: A woman 32 weeks pregnant has a worsening headache and spots in her vision. BP 178/112, HR 104, leg edema. No seizures yet.
critical.question: Diagnosis and transport risks?

options.t: Severe preeclampsia: left lateral, dim lights, seizure precautions, emergency transport to obstetrics

options.f: BP 160/110 or more with symptoms is severe.

options.t: Migraine: give paracetamol and stay home
options.f: Spots in the vision are a warning sign of eclampsia.

critical.explanation: Risks: eclampsia, stroke, placental abruption. Magnesium sulfate is given by ALS per protocol.
critical.kpi: Recognizes preeclampsia as a hypertensive emergency and implements seizure precautions

critical.scenario: A 63-year-old collapsed 10 minutes ago. Unresponsive with snoring, left-sided weakness. BP 198/118, HR 52, breathing 8 with pauses, SpO₂ 88%. Unequal pupils.
critical.question: What does this triad mean, and your priority?

options.t: Raised intracranial pressure (likely bleed): airway and ventilation, head up 30°, stroke centre with neurosurgery; don't lower BP
Inferior MI: aspirin and PCI centre
Give a drug to lower the BP
options.f: The BP is keeping blood flowing to the brain.

critical.explanation: Ventilate 10 breaths/min to EtCO₂ 35–45 mmHg; brief hyperventilation only for signs of herniation, per protocol.
critical.kpi: Recognizes Cushing's triad as a sign of elevated ICP and prioritizes neurological management over BP control
